extracted.intended_audience: public relations students, educators, and practicing PR professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for professionalism in public relations covering ethics (PRSA Code), the necessary body of knowledge, marks of scientific immaturity, curricular requirements for PR education, stages of professional education, and career competence levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of conflicting interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall disclose when an interest is or may be in conflict with a duty to a client or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure of such interests to all involved is required (text emphasizes disclosure before acting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguarding client confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall safeguard the confidence of both present and former clients or employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members shall not accept retainers or employment that may involve disclosure or use of these confidences to the disadvantage or prejudice of such clients or employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid practices that corrupt communication or government processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall not engage in any practice which tends to corrupt the integrity of channels of communication or the processes of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibits actions that would undermine institutional or public communication systems; no specific examples provided in this excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and care to avoid misleading information
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall not intentionally communicate false or misleading information and is obligated to use care to avoid communication of false or misleading information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This imposes both a prohibition on intentional deception and a due-diligence obligation to prevent inadvertent misleading communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify client or employer for public communications
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall be prepared to identify publicly the name of the client or employer on whose behalf any public communication is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires openness about for whom public messages are issued; relates to transparency and disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using undisclosed front organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall not make use of any individual or organization purporting to serve or represent an unannounced cause, or purporting to be independent or unbiased, but actually serving an undisclosed special or private interest of a member, client or employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbids use of 'astroturf' or secretly controlled advocacy groups; emphasizes disclosure of actual sponsorship or control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not intentionally injure another practitioner's reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall not intentionally injure the professional reputation or practice of another practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a member has evidence that another member has been guilty of unethical, illegal or unfair practices (including Code violations), the member shall present the information promptly to the proper Society authorities for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to testify in code enforcement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A member called as a witness in a proceeding for the enforcement of this Code shall be bound to appear, unless excused for sufficient reason by the Judicial Panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports enforceability of the professional code by requiring member cooperation with investigatory/judicial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure before accepting third-party payments
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall not accept fees, commissions or any other valuable consideration from anyone other than the client or employer in connection with those services without the express consent of the client or employer, given after a full disclosure of the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents hidden payments or conflicts of interest; requires client awareness and consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not guarantee results beyond member's control
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall not guarantee the achievement of specified results beyond the member's direct control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places realistic limits on promises and prevents misleading guarantees of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sever ties if required conduct would violate the Code
rubrics_metrics.description: A member shall, as soon as possible, sever relations with any organization or individual if such relationship requires conduct contrary to the articles of this Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates withdrawal from assignments or clients that would force unethical behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of organizational codes (enforceability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes of ethics exist (e.g., PRSA) and procedures for enforcement have been used, but most practitioners do not belong to PRSA and many members do not file complaints, limiting effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that codes alone cannot prohibit nonmembers and therefore professional status is limited by inability to control nonmembers' behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing is unlikely to produce effective control
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing of public relations practitioners has been proposed but is unlikely to work effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: constitutional protections for speech/press limit what licensing can achieve (only title control), states would need licensing boards creating red tape, and licensing would not necessarily keep out nonprofessionals in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for training and continuing education to promote ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Training of future practitioners and continuing education for current practitioners are necessary to help them be an ethical force in their organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position that education and ongoing professional development, not simply codes, will raise ethical behavior across the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of knowledge must be based on scholarly research, not anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there are many textbooks and journals, much of the published 'knowledge' in PR has been anecdotal; a profession requires facts achieved through research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Grunig-Hickson review found only a small fraction of items reporting scholarly research; the authors argue for more research-driven theory applicable to PR practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize personal experience into testable theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal experiences and practitioner anecdotes should be organized into coherent theory which is then tested to determine its ability to solve public relations problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests combining practitioner experience, concepts from social sciences, and communication research to build and empirically test PR theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks of an immature/undeveloped science
rubrics_metrics.description: An immature and undeveloped science can be recognized by: (1) absence of facts achieved through research; (2) reliance on 'folk science' rather than verified principles; (3) emphasis on exchange of personal impressions in education rather than widely accepted theory; (4) inconclusive research and scholarly activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four characteristics (from Ravetz model as applied by Van Slyke) are diagnostic criteria to assess the maturity of PR as a scientific/professional field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations curriculum — broad liberal education
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations students should receive a broad liberal education; accrediting council requires about 75% of courses be outside the communications unit, and most of the first two years should be outside PR/communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports claims that liberal arts training helps students understand the world and be better PR professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations curriculum — communication skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need communication skills (writing, editing, design) and courses that apply journalistic skills to PR problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry-level jobs require journalistic skills; even higher-level people must have mastered communication skills before moving to management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations curriculum — knowledge for management
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need knowledge to manage PR: theories of communication applied to planning and management, behavior of publics, research methods, and evaluation techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers the managerial and theoretical knowledge (Parts I–III of the book) needed for higher-level PR roles beyond craft skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations curriculum — knowledge of the employing organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must understand the organization for which they work (business, government, non-profit) so they can serve as boundary persons interpreting organization to publics and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for placing PR programs in or connected to relevant university units (business, public administration, etc.) or encouraging minors in related fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations curriculum — practical experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should gain practical experience through supervised internships and senior 'campaigns' courses where they examine case studies and develop PR programs for real organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical experience results in better job placement and prepares students for entry-level and advanced roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR education stages and need to reach Stage III
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional education progresses through three stages: Stage I (apprenticeship outside formal education), Stage II (apprenticeship inside formal education), Stage III (scholar-teacher researches, analyzes, and criticizes the profession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue PR education must move to Stage III—where scholarship informs practice—before PR can reach full professional maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities/professional programs must sustain the intellectual tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: PR programs must conduct research, criticize the profession, and carry on the intellectual tradition of the university to gain status and contribute to a genuine liberal education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without research and critical scholarship, PR programs risk being marginalized as vocational training and lacking university legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four career competence levels (PRSA guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRSA's career guide defines four levels of professional competence: Level I Beginning Professional, Level II Staff Professional, Level III Professional Manager, Level IV Senior Professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each level specifies typical duties and experience: Level I — introductory training/junior staff; Level II — junior management, specialist (18–24 months after Level I); Level III — middle management, directs staff, research/planning (≥5 years at Level II); Level IV — top management/adviser/policymaker (up to 10 years at Level III). Use the levels to plan continuing education and career development.
